Paver Driveways · Apopka, FL

Paver Driveways for Apopka's Growing Subdivisions

Figure $10–$30 per sq ft installed for a paver driveway in Apopka heading into the last quarter of 2026. Orange County's second-largest city added nearly 11,000 residents between 2020 and mid-2025, and a meaningful share of the paver driveways going in today are first installs on recently built lots rather than a swap for a cracked original.

By the Opera Concrete & Pavers estimating team · Updated October 1, 2026

Pavers don't get a lighter permit path than poured concrete

Apopka's own trigger for a building permit covers altering, repairing or adding any structure on the lot without carving out an exception for material (the city's Building Permit FAQ). A paver driveway goes through the Building-Safety Department's review the same as a poured one, with the fee again set at $7.50 per $1,000 of contract value against a $75 floor (Apopka Permitting Fees).

A driveway built to carry more than a sedan

A standard residential paver driveway is built around the loads a car puts on it, but a boat trailer, an RV, or a loaded work truck asks more of the same surface. ICPI's spec response is layered: a thicker 80 mm paver instead of the usual 60 mm, a base compacted to the stricter modified Proctor standard used for vehicular areas rather than the pedestrian number, and edge restraint that can actually hold the field together under a turning tire. None of those changes are visible once the job is finished, part of why they're easy to skip on a Apopka quote that never asks what the driveway will actually carry. Specifying the load up front is cheaper than rebuilding a surface that wasn't built for it.

A paver driveway on a newly platted lot, worked out in square feet

A 24 by 24 ft paver driveway on a new-construction lot comes to 576 sq ft. At $10–$30 per sq ft installed, that job runs roughly $5,760 to $17,280 depending on the paver and base depth chosen. On a freshly graded lot, the base crew is usually working with fill that hasn't settled through a full wet season yet, so compaction gets checked carefully before the bedding sand and pavers go down, a step that matters less on an older, already-settled lot nearby.

A fast-growing city means more first installs than replacements

The Census Bureau's latest estimate puts Apopka's population at 65,552 as of July 1, 2025, up from 54,892 in 2020, a jump of close to 20 percent in five years (Census Bureau, Vintage 2025 population estimates). Wikipedia describes the city, citing Census data, as "expanding in all directions" (Wikipedia, Apopka, Florida), which tracks with what a paver crew sees on the ground: more driveways poured onto fresh fill for the first time than pulled out and replaced.

Efflorescence: the white haze that isn't a defect

A whitish, powdery bloom can appear on new concrete pavers within about 60 days of installation, and ICPI's own spec is direct about what it is: a calcium carbonate deposit that does not affect the structural performance or durability of the pavers. It can look alarming on a dark paver especially, and a driveway installed during a dry stretch near Apopka may not show it at all until the first real rain of the wet season brings it out. It usually fades with weather and traffic over time and isn't something a sealer is required to fix. Mistaking it for a flaw in the material, rather than a normal early-life process, is the most common false alarm on a new paver driveway.

What a 98 percent Proctor reading actually means for a Apopka driveway

ICPI calls for the compacted subgrade and the aggregate base under a driveway to reach at least 98 percent of standard Proctor density, tested against ASTM D698, with vehicular areas held to the stricter modified Proctor instead. That number comes from a plate compactor working the base in lifts of 4 to 6 inches, not one pass over the whole excavation. Skipping a lift, or compacting a lift that's too thick, is how a base looks finished on the surface and still settles under Apopka traffic within a season. The spec also sets a surface tolerance of plus or minus three-eighths of an inch over 10 feet, tighter than it sounds once pavers sit on top of it.

Inspections on a driveway, if the job needs one

Florida law keeps a local government from requiring a license just to install a driveway, but that doesn't remove the permit itself, and a permit usually comes with an inspection tied to it. Projects with a direct contract price over $2,500 also fall under Florida's lien law, which requires a recorded Notice of Commencement before work starts, separate from any building-permit inspection. Whether a specific Apopka driveway needs a permit at all depends on the scope, the jurisdiction, and whether the work touches a right-of-way apron, which is worth asking the local building department directly rather than assuming the answer from a different town's rule.

What to do about an oil stain, fast

Because concrete pavers aren't sealed by default, an oil or fluid stain soaks in rather than sitting on the surface, so the fastest response, blotting the spill right away rather than wiping it or letting it sit, matters more on an unsealed Apopka driveway than it would on a sealed one. A stain that's already set can sometimes be lifted with a degreaser made for masonry, applied and worked in rather than pressure-washed aggressively, since high pressure aimed straight at the joints risks the same sand loss a routine cleaning causes. Sealing the driveway ahead of time, even without a fixed resealing schedule required, is the more direct way to keep future spills from reaching the paver at all.

Frequently asked questions

Does a paver driveway in Apopka need a different permit than a concrete one?

No. The city's permit trigger applies to any structure regardless of material, so a paver driveway goes through the same Building-Safety Department review and fee formula a poured driveway would.

Is most paver driveway work in Apopka new construction or replacement?

A larger share than in many older Central Florida cities is new construction, since the city's population grew nearly 20 percent between 2020 and mid-2025 on a wave of new subdivisions.

Does fresh fill on a new Apopka lot change how a paver base gets built?

It can. Soil on a recently graded lot hasn't always settled through a full wet season, so a crew checks compaction more carefully there than on an older, already-settled lot.
